clue.text: A difficult crossword book

parts.note: something difficult is hard
the Times is a newspaper famous for its crossword, so a crossword can be called a Times

explanation.surface: A puzzle book of fiendish crosswords.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A difficult crossword book' reads as one description, but 'book' alone is the definition; the Times newspaper is famed for its crossword. Hard Times is a Dickens novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Hard Times is a novel by Charles Dickens, published in 1854.

clue.text: See 26
Welshman holding cask does not reveal content

indicators.note: the Welshman holds the cask, so its letters wrap around the other piece

parts.note: Rees is a common Welsh surname, standing for a Welshman
a pin is a small cask holding four and a half gallons

explanation.surface: A Welshman clutching a barrel keeps quiet about what is inside it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'content' looks like the contents of the cask, but it is the adjective: one who frets is showing he is not content.
explanation.definitionFit: To fret and complain is to display discontent, so such a person plainly is not content.

clue.text: Plot development in second part of novel

definitions.meaning: an unexpected turn in a story
the second word of Dickens's novel title Oliver ...

explanation.surface: A surprise arriving midway through a novel.
explanation.definitionFit: A surprising turn of plot is a twist, and the surname completes Dickens's Oliver Twist.

clue.text: Heroine loses a ring in wild country

indicators.note: the wild country gives up one of its letters, so something is removed

parts.note: moorland is open, wild upland country
O is shaped like a ring

explanation.surface: A heroine drops her ring somewhere out on the moors.
explanation.walkthrough: Catherine Morland is the heroine of Jane Austen's Northanger Abbey; the puzzle's unclued theme is Austen heroines.
explanation.definitionFit: Catherine Morland is the central character of Austen's novel Northanger Abbey.

clue.text: Wonderful month goes with a big bang

parts.note: super is an informal word for wonderful
Nov is the abbreviation of November

explanation.surface: A splendid month that ends with a celebratory explosion.
explanation.definitionFit: An exploding star produces an enormous blast of light and energy, a cosmic explosion.

clue.text: Heroines — pursued without energy

parts.note: the punctuation mark in the clue is itself a dash

indicators.note: the pursuing word goes without a letter, which is removed

parts.note: a suitor who pursued someone romantically wooed them
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A band of heroines, once chased, now run out of steam.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed dash is not just punctuation: it supplies its own name. Elinor and Marianne Dashwood are the heroines of Sense and Sensibility, hence the plural.
explanation.definitionFit: The two sisters of Austen's Sense and Sensibility share this surname, so it names a pair of heroines.

clue.text: Not all clothes end in tatters, coming from China

indicators.note: not all of the word is used, so its final letter is dropped

parts.note: a dress is an item of clothing

indicators.note: torn to tatters, the letters of 'end' are torn up and rearranged

explanation.surface: Clothing ending up in shreds after coming from China.
explanation.walkthrough: 'China' looks like the country, but here it is porcelain; 'in tatters' rearranges END into DEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Dresden is a type of fine porcelain, made at Meissen near Dresden, so it is a kind of china.

clue.text: Was judge burning to talk to underling?

indicators.note: spoken out, sat alight gives the sound of the answer

parts.note: a judge sat on the bench, so was judge means sat; something burning is alight

explanation.surface: A judge in a fury, keen to tear into a junior.
explanation.walkthrough: 'burning to talk to' looks like eagerness, but 'to talk' signals that SAT ALIGHT is spoken, sounding like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A satellite is a follower or dependant who revolves around a more powerful figure, a subordinate.

clue.text: Raise pincers back to front: where does one get those from?

definitions.text: where does one get those from?

indicators.note: the letter at the back of the combined pieces is shifted to the front

parts.note: to raise is to put up
pliers are pincers for gripping

explanation.surface: Someone lifting pliers the wrong way round wonders where they were bought.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back to front' looks like turning the pincers round, but only the final S moves to the front of UPPLIERS.
explanation.definitionFit: A firm that provides goods is where one obtains them, so it answers the question of their source.

clue.text: Instruction to players in northern team when one short

indicators.note: the team is one letter short, so its last letter is dropped

parts.note: Preston North End is a football club from Lancashire in the north of England

explanation.surface: Orders given to a northern side down to ten men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'players' looks like footballers but means musicians.
explanation.definitionFit: Presto is a musical direction telling performers to play very fast.

clue.text: Criminal kidnaps extremely naive heroine

indicators.note: the criminal seizes the other letters and holds them inside

parts.note: bent is slang for crooked or criminal

indicators.note: only the extreme letters of the word are taken

explanation.surface: A crook abducts a very innocent young heroine.
explanation.definitionFit: Elizabeth Bennet is the heroine of Austen's Pride and Prejudice.

clue.text: Maybe pet, having got dry, needs drink

parts.note: laundry that has aired has been dried out
ale is beer

explanation.surface: A pet after a towelling-off is ready for a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: The Airedale is a large terrier breed, and a dog is an example of a pet.

clue.text: Did a little jogging, almost free

indicators.note: almost all of the phrase is used, so its last letter goes

parts.note: someone who did a little jogging ran some

explanation.surface: A short jog that came close to costing nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: To ransom a captive is to pay to have them set free.

clue.text: One plated up, giving off aroma including herb

indicators.note: the jumbled letters take the herb inside them
an aroma gone off is spoiled, so its letters are jumbled

parts.note: dill is a herb

explanation.surface: A dish served up with a herb, smelling off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plated up' looks like food on a plate; it means covered in armour plates. 'giving off' makes ARMAO from the aroma letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The animal is covered in bony armour plates, so it is a creature plated up.

clue.text: Woman heartily contrite, suffering a lot of weight

indicators.note: only the heart, the central letter, of the word is taken
the contrite letters suffer and are rearranged

explanation.surface: A deeply sorry woman bears a heavy burden.
explanation.definitionFit: A unit of a thousand kilograms is a large measure of mass.

clue.text: One said to be dead cross about love receiving answer

indicators.note: the cross is turned about, read backwards

parts.note: a rood is a crucifix or cross

indicators.note: the zero receives a letter inside it

parts.note: love is nil, zero in tennis scoring

explanation.surface: A dead person, angry about a love affair, gets a reply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cross' looks like angry; it is a crucifix, ROOD, turned round by 'about'.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'dead as a doornail' makes this object the proverbial dead thing.

clue.text: Gave news of my divorce?

definitions.meaning: read as ..., the speaker splitting up

explanation.surface: Announcing that one's marriage has ended.
explanation.definitionFit: To impart information is to pass it on, and 'I'm parted' describes someone divorced.

clue.text: Not being pure, program gave false answer

parts.note: an app is a software program
one who lied gave an untrue answer

explanation.surface: A corrupt computer program that told untruths.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pure' suggests moral purity, but it is the scientist's contrast of pure and practical research.
explanation.definitionFit: Applied mathematics or science is the practical kind, as opposed to pure theory.

clue.text: Such a worker dealing with admin extremely crisply?

indicators.note: the letters are dealt out like cards, mixed into a new order
only the outer letters of the word are taken

explanation.surface: An energetic employee getting through paperwork briskly.
explanation.walkthrough: The ends of 'crisply' are scattered through the result, so they go into the pool for 'dealing' rather than sitting beside it.
explanation.definitionFit: An energetic, forceful worker is described with this adjective, so the clue asks what kind of worker.

clue.text: Author brings a number to the Guardian

parts.note: the clue appears in the Guardian, so the paper speaking of itself is us
ten is a number

explanation.surface: A writer submits a figure to the newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The newspaper refers to itself, so 'the Guardian' gives US, as 'we' would.
explanation.definitionFit: Jane Austen is the novelist whose heroines are this puzzle's theme.

clue.text: As welcome to elite force, I'm passed up raw flesh to eat

parts.note: the SAS is the British Army's Special Air Service
hi is a greeting of welcome

indicators.note: in a down clue, passed up means read upwards, backwards

explanation.surface: A special forces soldier greeted and handed raw meat.
explanation.definitionFit: This Japanese dish consists of thin slices of uncooked fish.

clue.text: A possibility of acquiring a daughter?

definitions.text: A possibility of acquiring a daughter?

indicators.note: the pieces take in a letter, acquiring it inside

parts.note: an option is a possibility

explanation.surface: One way of gaining a daughter.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking a child legally into one's family is a way to gain a daughter.

clue.text: Man judge hopes will swing

indicators.note: the hopes swing about, their letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A judge hoping a man will hang.
explanation.definitionFit: Joseph is a man's name, so it stands for an example of a man.

clue.text: Military rulers some days need appreciation

parts.note: Jun, short for June, is a month, a set of days
ta is British informal for thank you

explanation.surface: Generals in power occasionally want thanking.
explanation.definitionFit: A junta is a military group ruling a country after seizing power.

clue.text: Heroine's parking on the grass

parts.note: P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking
rice is a cereal grass

explanation.surface: A heroine leaving her car on the lawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heroine's' is 'Heroine is'. Fanny Price is the heroine of Austen's Mansfield Park.
explanation.definitionFit: Fanny Price is the central character of Austen's Mansfield Park.

clue.text: Poet has extra line for heroine

indicators.note: the poet's name takes an extra letter inside it

parts.note: T. S. Eliot was a poet

explanation.surface: A poet adds another line about a heroine.
explanation.definitionFit: Anne Elliot is the heroine of Austen's Persuasion.

clue.text: Dwarf's back home wearing shortened swimming costume

indicators.note: the costume is worn around the other piece, which goes inside
the costume is cut short, losing its last letter

parts.note: a mankini is a skimpy one-piece male swimsuit

indicators.note: the word is read back to front

parts.note: being in means being at home

explanation.surface: A little man back at home in a skimpy swimsuit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dwarf's' is 'Dwarf is', a link. A mankini is a skimpy one-piece swimsuit for men, made famous by the film Borat.
explanation.definitionFit: A mannikin is a very small person, a little man.

clue.text: Heroine wanted to speak to Parliament

indicators.note: spoken out, the word would gives a sound like a timber word

parts.note: 'would' can mean wanted, as in 'would that it were so'
the House of Commons, or either chamber, is a house

explanation.surface: A heroine eager to address Parliament.
explanation.definitionFit: Emma Woodhouse is the heroine of Austen's Emma.

clue.text: Drink bowl of soup noisily; this 1 of 5 a day?

indicators.note: said noisily, out loud, the pieces give the answer's sound

parts.note: to neck is British slang for to drink quickly; a tureen is a deep serving bowl for soup

explanation.surface: Slurping soup from the bowl as part of a healthy diet.
explanation.walkthrough: '5 a day' is the UK health advice to eat five portions of fruit and vegetables daily.
explanation.definitionFit: The fruit is one of the five daily portions of fruit and vegetables recommended.
